Sat 20 Jan 1877 - Adelaide Observer (SA : 1843 - 1904) 

Page 11 - KINGSTON AND MARRACOORTE RAILWAY.

On this Page 11

KINGSTON AND NARRACOORTE

RAILWAY.

[From our Special Reporter.]

A most important event in the history of the

South-Eastern District, and one of considerable

moment in connection with the scheme of rail-

way extension which South Australia is now bent

upon carrying out, took place on the 16th

instant, when the railway from Kingston to

Narracoorte was formally opened by the

Commissioner of Public Works and brought into

use for locomotive traction. Unlike that which

was inaugurated some weeks since by His

Excellency the Governor, the present line is

unconnected with the South Australian railway

system which was provided for during the last

session of Parliament. Though a branch is at

present proposed, and others will doubtless be

decided on, it is isolated from the general

system; but in spite of that fact it must be to

the people of the South-East a source of consi-

derable satisfaction, inasmuch as it will tend to

bring trade to the South Australian coast which

would have gone undoubtedly to Victoria,

besides rendering travelling easy over a very

difficult country. Twelve years ago the mail

from Adelaide to Mount Gambier was four

days and four nights on the road, and

passengers on that line will have a

vivid recollection of the portion of the journey

lying between Kingston and Narracoorte as

being without exception the worst country to

travel through in the whole of the colony. In

summer the greater portion of the distance was

made over deep dry sand, and in winter the

traveller had to make his way over flats covered

with water up to the horses' knees for miles in

succession. The other portions of the road from

Adelaide to Mount Gambier are bad, but those

who are most intimately acquainted with the

country between Kingston and Narracoorte

speak in the most decided manner of its being

by far the most difficult on the route. The

Kingston and Narracoorte Railway will have

the effect of bridging over this soure of general

discomfort and inconvenience, and its construc-

tion will no doubt be hailed with delight by

travellers.

It will be at once seen that to make a railway

over such peculiar country was a work of no

ordinary difficulty, as communications had to be

made good from each end, and only six months of

the year were practically available for carrying

on operations. The necessity of the work became

obvious when the importance was seen of getting a

good port for the country lying to the north and

east of Narracoorte, which has been unoccupied

or only very partially occupied owing to the

want of means of communication with the sea

board. Indeed the principal thing that the

South-East required was good harbour accom-

modation—in other words, a proper and safe sea

port ; and from the absence of such a port it was

found impossible to load ships for England

direct. Port MacDonnell is admitted even by

its friends to be unsafe, and the same is the

case with Robe. Kingston or Port Caroline is,

however, known as a safe port, suitable for

vesels of any size. In order to render Kingston

available the tract of bad country which lay

between it and the settled lands had to be bridged

over, and this has now been done by the con-

struction of the Kingston and Narracoorte

Railway.

Much of our railway legislation has been beset

with difficulties and rendered slow by reason of

the action of rival political parties. The legis

lation out of which the Kingston and Narra

coorte Railway sprang was of this kind. There

were parties in the House generally in favour of

railway construction in the South-East to

connect the good areas there with the seaboard;

but one set of politicians believed in attracting

the traffic to the Mount Gambier end, while

another saw only Lacepede Bay as the point of

shipment. The result was a great deal

of discussion in Parliament over Bills which

came to grief or were not carried out when

passed. Had our politicians been told when the

Narracoorte and Kingston Railway was first

mooted in Parliament how many years would

«lapse before the work would be accomplished

we think they .would not have believed that

their purpose would so long have remained

unfulfilled. The question of railway communi

cation iu tiie South-East was agitated by

private persons a number of years ago. A few

words will suffice to show what was done with

the question in Parliament. On October 23,

1866, the late Mr. J. H. Barrow tabled a motion

in the Legislative Council affirming the desira

bility of making certain railways in the colony,

amongst them a line to the South-East via

Strathalbyn. The motion was amended by

the Hon. T. Magarey so as to include

a railway in the South-East amongst those stated

to be desirable, and in that form it was carried.

In the following session the construction of a

railway from Lacepede Bay to the Victorian

Border with a branch to Narracoorte was

shadowed forth in the viceregal speech, and on

September 25 a message was brought down

recommending an advance out of the General

Revenue of £270,000 for the work, to be paid

out of any loan raised for the purpose. The

Hon. P. Santo was then Commissioner of Public

Works. It was evident that the Government

intended to cons tract the Mount Gambier end

-of the line first. Mr. Oolton, who was in the

Assembly, moved an amendment, and spoke in

support of the Lacepede Bay and Narracoorte

portion of a line to Mount Gambier being

first made. The amendment was, however,

lost, the motion agreed to, and the Mount

Gambier and Narracoorte Railway Bill was

brought in and passed on October 16, 1867.

Those who most favoured this Bill urged as

their strong point the great difficulty of the

. country between Kingston and Narracoorte.

^ ® need not stay to tell what this measure

proposed to do, inasmuch as it never was carried

into effect, though still on the Statute-Book.

In the next session the Government informed

the House that as they had found it would be

cheaper to land railway material at Lacepede

Bay than at Port MacDonnell they did not in

tend going on with the Mount Gambier and

Narracoorte line till hon. members had had an

opportunity of considering a Bill for construct

ing a railway from Lacepede Bay to Narra

coorte. Nothing further was done during

that year. In December. 1868, the late Ron.

T. Reynolds tabled a motion in the House in

favour of the South Australian Government

guaranteeing a certain amount of interest on

the outlay of any Company that would con

struct a line from Port Caroline (Kingston) to

Port MacDonnell by way of Narracoorte, Penola,

and Mount Gambier. Mr. Bower, however,

amended the motion bo as merely to express

the desirability of obtaining information, and

in that form it was carried. An attempt was

made by Mr. Pearce to pass a resolution for the

.introduction of a Bill similar to that desired by

the Hon. T. Reynolds; but it was postponed,

and afterwards withdrawn at the request of

the Government of the day. On No

vember 18, 1869, Mr. Colton, then Com

missioner of Public Works of the Strangways

'Government, moved a preliminary motion for

the introduction of a Bill for a locomotive tram

way between Lacepede and MacDonnell Bays,

via Narracoorte, Penola, and Mount Gambier,

by means of a guarantee not exceeding 5J per

?cent, on the amount required. The motion was,

.carried, but the Bill by an oversight was passed

by the House before the necessary message from

the Governor had been sent down. The measure

was returned from the Council. The passing

motion was rescinded by the House, and the

Bill passed again; but it was considered a fresh

measure when it reached the Council again, and

beforejthe second reading could be taken a poli

tical crisis intervened, and it fell amongst the

slaughtered innocents. In the session of 1870-1

nothing was done on this subject, though one

debate occurred upon the motion in general terms.

Leave was obtained by Mr. Carr, then Commis-

sioner of Public Works, on August 16,1871, to

bring in the Bill under which the work b« been

constructed. The measure, of which the second

reading was moved in the House on September

14 of the same year, was for a horse railway

from lacepede Bay to Narracoorte. The cost of

the railway proposed two years previously was

to be £5,000 per mile, but this was estimated at

only £2,900, on the 3 feet 6 inch gauge. The

gauge question on this as on other Railway Bills

.was fruitful in debates,and on the third reading

we find Mr. A. F. Lindsay movijg the previous

question. The measure was, however, carried

by a majority of two to one in the House, the

second reading being passed by 18 against nine,

and the third by 10 against five, and having

passed the Council the measure received the

Royal assent on November 23, 1871.

A survey had been made for a line from King

ston to the Border, with a branch to Narra

coorte by Mount Babbage ; but the direct line

from Kingston to Narracoorte was ultimately

adopted. The working survey for Jthe contract

drawings was made under the direction of Mr.

Hull. Some deviations were afterwards found

advisable during the construction of the work.

The line 'was divided into three sections; and

contracts were let for the earthworks exclusive

of the permanent way. The first section in

cluded the wet flats between Kingston and

Reedy Creek Bange, and was fifteen miles long.

The second extended twenty miles, and the thirtl

covered the remainder of the 52J miles.

Messrs. J. C. & J. Leonard were successful

tenderers for the first, sections two and

three being carried out by Messrs. Paltridgeand

Parkin. Operations were begun in April, 1873

The first section was completed in June, 1875

and the second and third respectively in July

and December of the same year. Although the

time taken was apparently long, yet when we

consider that work was practically suspended

for six months of each year; that owing to the

difficulty of keeping up communication and of

obtaining labour from the isolated character

of the district, the time, we think, will compare

favourably with that taken for similar

works in other parts of the colony.

From the taking out of the first barrowful of

stuff to the opening of the line for horse trac

tion the time occupied was three years and

three months; and taking into consideration

the length of the line-52§ miles-and the

character of the country through which the

railway passes, there has been no instance in the

railway construction of the colony in which a

greater amount of work has been done in the

same time except in the case of the railway from

Boseworthy to the Burra, which was made at a

time when labour was much more plentiful.

The laying of the permanent way was com

menced in April, 1S75, and was finished in

twelve months from that time; Mr. Bampton,

now one of the Inspectors on the Northern line,

being employed as Superintendent, and the

sidings and station arrangements being subse

quently completed under the superintendence of

Mr. Puddy, now inspector of the Permanent way.

It had been first intended to work the traffic

by horse traction, but in the session of

1875 the Legislature determined to employ

steam, and the necessary engines and

other appurtenances were ordered from .

England. The engines not having arrived j

when the permanent way was finished the line

could not at once be utilized as proposed; but

in order to accommodate the people about

Narracoorte who wished to transport a consi- ?

derable quantity of wheat to the seaboard, it

was decided by the Government that horse

traction should be temporarily provided.

"While the proceedings in connection with this

arrangement were going forward there was a

change of Ministry, so that two Commissioners .

of Public Works had a finger in the pie. A

representation was made by the inhabitants when

Mr. Boucaut was Commissioner. We believe

that he gave instructions that their request

should be complied with, and that when the

necessary documents were taken to his successor.

Mr. Colton, the present Commissioner, took a 1

similar view. Traffic began in last June. On

the 1st August following the carriage of mails

and passengers by road from Kingston to Narra- |

coorte was discontinued. A passenger truck

then began to run, and continued up to the

present, to the great delight of those who have

much coacli travelling. ]

Up to the present time the results of the j

traffic, even under very inconvenient arrange- j

ments, have exceeded the estimate formed of it I

by the Government. In connection with this |

subject one noticeable fact has to be staged, j

The shipment of wool at Kingston for the j

season of 1875 amounted, we believe, to only

5,000 or 6,000 bales, and already during the

present season the number of bales shipped has

reached nearly 12,000. A portion of this large 1

excess consists of wool which was formerly

taken to Port MacDonnell, and the remainder is ;

Victorian wool, which was shipped previously at ;

Portland. There is, in fact, every reason to

believe that the traffic with the Victorian side

of the Border will be largely increased next j

year, when arrangements on the railway j

are complete. So far the present ex

periments have been sufficiently successful

to induce settlers there to promise the line their

patronage next season, and such trade will

doubtless be very materially increased when the

new jetty at Kingston in contemplation by the

Government is constructed, so as to enable

vessels to come alongside to load, and save the

heavy expense of lighterage.

With regard to the cost of the railway,

we may say that the original vote for the line was

£160,000, but at that time horse traction was

intended. In order to make the necessary

additions to convert it into a locomotive rail

way an additional sum of £40,000 was found

necessary, and bonds were issued. Deducting

the loss on the sale of bonds the

actual cost of the line is about £185,000, or

£3,525 per mile. This includes four loco

motive engines, 50 wagons, two passenger

carriages, break vans, good sheds at Kingston

and Narracoorte, which cost about £1,200

each, small passenger stations at the respective

termini, and four roadside stations, with cot-

tages for the station-masters, and other necessary

appurtenanees. The stations and cottages are

of wood, sheathed with galvanized iron.

In the construction of the line the object

has been to provide the essentials of a first-class

locomotive railway suitable for heavy traffic;

but only for the present to make use of pro-

visional arrangements adapted to compara

tively light work. With this view the

earthworks and gradients are equal to those

of any line in the colony. The steepest gradient

is only one in a hundred, and that occurs only in

one or two places, while the sharpest curve a

radius of 40 chains. The station-yards are also of

sufficient capacity to allow of any probable

future extension of traffic, while the the rails

and rolling-stock generally are of a light

description adapted to the present traffic and

intended to be altogether changed at some

future time. The rails weigh 35 lbs. to the

yard, the joints being fished and the line

thoroughly well sleepered and ballasted. The

weight of the engines is 12 tons in steam.

They are four in number and of the latest

description, adapted to the weight of the rails.

It is said that they will only take a limited

load at a slow rate of speed, but they are fully

equal to the probable requirements of the traffic

for some years to come. The locomotives were

made by Messrs. Bear, Peacock, & Co., of Man

chester, and cost about £1,450 each, including

freight to Adelaide. The carriages were built

at the Government Railway Workshops, and

they are mounted on iron under-frames, with end

platforms after the American fashion, and re

versible seats. The wagons have also iron under

frames, with steel axles, wrought-iron wheels,

and Beuther's patent oil-boxes; the bodies being

of Baltic deal, jarrah jarrah, or blackwood. The

wagons have cost about £130 each. Messrs.

Brown, Marshall, & Co., of Leeds, have

supplied the ironwork, the woodwork being

done in the colony. Two excellent turn

tables have been placed at the ends of the line.

They were manufactured by Messrs. Cowans,

Sheldon & Co., of Carlisle.

Owing to the wet nature of the country the cul

verts or flood-openings, especially on the lower

portion of the line, are unusually numerous and

large, varying from 100 to 5 feet in width. To pro

vide against the floods of winter drains have been

cut along the sides of the railway, and with

great effect. The peculiar character of the

country is farther shown by Hie wicker-work

which has been found necessary to keep the.

water from washing away the- sides of' the per

manent way in passing through the swampy

country near 'Kingston. The bridges proper are

only three in number-over Beedy, Mosquito,

and Narracoorte Creeks. The Reedy Creek

Bridge is 90 feet span in six bays, with timber

piers and stone abutments. There are

also over the same, creek three subsidiary

bridges, one of 20 and two of 30 feet span,

making in all 170 feet. A skew bridge of a

similar description is provided at Mosquito

Creek of 80 feet span. That over the Narracoorte

Creek has a span of 60 feet. The bridges are

all of rough timber framing, designed solely

with a view to the weight that they will have

to carry. No expenditure has therefore taken

place in ornamentation. The line has been

constructed throughout under the immediate

supervision of Mr. Bogers, Government Assis

tant-Engineer for the South-Bast District.

In addition to the terminal stations at

Kingston and Narracoorte there are, as we

before stated, four intermediate stations. Pro

ceeding from the east, and in the direction of

Narracoorte, the first is at Beedy Creek, about

12 miles from Kingston; the second at Avenue

Range, about 20 miles up; the third at Baker's

Range, 31 miles from Kingston; and the fourth

at Stewart's Range, about 45 miles. The

terminal stations especially have been left as

mere skeletons of important stations to

be filled in hereafter. At the Kingston end

there are two townships-that of Kingston,

which has been a long time established and is

the centre of population; and the township of

Port Caroline, which the Government have laid

out. These are divided by a small range of

sandhills, through which the railway runs. There

are two distinct railway yards at Kingston

one on the seaward side of the sandbank near

the jetty, and one on the eastern side. A tempo

rary passenger station and the goods station are

erected in the yard on the Port Caroline side,

but it is anticipated that as traffic extends the

permanent station will be fixed on that higher

up, only goods traffic being taken on through

the sandhills; and as there are two level

crossings in the township this, seems to be

the safer plan to adopt. The workshops

will also be erected on the Kingston side of the

sandhill, as the position of the other yard is un

suitable owing to the drift. Besides these

reasons in favour of the opening up of a second

yard, we are told that the length of station

yard obtainable near the jetty would not be

sufficient for future traffic, and that the passen

ger station will be nearer the majority of the

inhabitants when placed in the Kingston yard.

The railway yard at Narracoorte is twenty-six

acres in extent, and the terminus is so placed

that the line may be extended, passing between

the townships of Narracoorte and Kincraig

without touching on them to any material

extent, either to Border Town or the Vic

torian Border. The question of the site of the

Narracoorte terminus is one upon which a good

deal of dissatisfaction prevails. At the Narra

coorte end of the line there are also two town

ships-Kincraig, an old private township; and

Narracoorte, which was laid out some years ago

by the South Australian Government. These

are divided by the creek, and Kincraig joins

Narracoorte on its south-eastern side ; so that the

two townships form two sides of a square, and

the Bailway Station is fixed in the re-entering

angle between the two. The passenger shed is

on the western end of the railway yard, and a

new approach has been formed to the town

ship of Narracoorte, branching from the

main road to Bobe. The goods station

stands nearly at the centre of the

station-yard, and a new road "ha-s been formed

along the back in continuation of the main

road to Apsley, which will serve as an approach

to the goods station jfrom Kincraig, where the

greater part of the business is at present

carried on. The original site of the terminus

shown on the Parliamentary plan was in the

angle of the road between Narracoorte and Bobe

lying to the south-west of the former township;

but this was liapily changed in the construction

of the railway, and the line brought nearer to

Kincraig than was contempleted when the cost

was estimated by 35 chains. That extension

has been made, firstly, with a view to the con

venience of the inhabitants of Kincraig;

secondly, to secure a site for the station, from

which the line could be extended at any future

time in an easterly direction without the

expense which would be involved by going

through the townships; and thirdly, in order to

secure sufficient room for the very extensive

sidings which may probably become necessary in

the event of Narracoorte becoming the changing

station for the through traffic between Victoria

and Kingston. That there must be a changing

place at Narracoorte, or between there and the

Border, is the very unpleasant fact which is

forced upon us by the non-adoption of the 5

feet 3 inch gauge, which is the gauge of the

Victorian railways. It seems a great pity, in the

event of a heavy Victorian traffic, that the

broader gauge was not at once agreed to, for it

seems very" possible that a few years hence

.^he change will become necessary, In which case

the rails and rolling-stock will be rendered

absolutely useless. Looking at the probable

changes and extensions of the future, and at

Narracoorte as a populous township, which it

may be expected to become, and also taking

into consideration the space required for sidings

in case it is made a changing station where the

break of gauge shall occur, the station does not

appear to be inappropriately placed. If a great

mistake seems to have been made, and one about

which the inhabitants of Kincraig have good

cause for complaint, it was made by the Govern

ment that declared the Township of Narracoorte,

necessitating the placing of public buildings

there when the population was gathered in Kin'

craig. There seems, however, no doubt now

that Narracoorte will extend, and when this is

the case, as we have said, the passenger station

will be found conveniently situated. For in

laying out railways the future has to be looked

to as well as the present.

Such opposite views have been and are

still taken with regard to the probable

traffic that we have thought it well to enquire

into tiie matter. In order to speak of the nature

of the traffic expected, we will take the four

stations on the line consecutively. Beedy Creek

Station can never receive any other trade than

will come from a few sheep stations lying to the

north and south of it on the Bsedy Creek

Bange. The Avenue Range Station will

probably have a more important effect upon the

business of the line. To the north there is a

considerable quantity of land either absolutely

fit for cultivation at present or capable of being

made so by drainage. To the south of Crower,

at £a distance of about eight miles, begins an

exceedingly fine tract of country, which

promises to be equal in fertility to any in the

South-Bast. At Baker's Bange a large area of

land has already been surveyed. "We believe

about 30,000 acres have been selected, and it is

intended to throw open about 20,000 acres

more in a few months. The quantity of really

good agricultural land is stated to be only about

5,000 acres, but the selectors will possess the

great additional advantage of extensive

commonage. There seems to be no reason

why this land should not be profitably occupied

in large blocks under the system of combining

pastoral with agricultural farming, which is

now beginning to be extensively and we believe

profitably practised in' the South-East. After

leaving Baker's Bange a tract of worthless,

miserable country, locally termed the Heath, is

passed through, which continues to the station

at Stewart's Bange, situated on the western

side of the Mosquito Plains. This station will

receive the traffic from Morambro, in the North,

and from the fanning country on the same

range lying to the south. It is a fact much to

be regretted that the land here was alienated

prior to the construction of the railway, and

that the greater portion has fallen back

into the hands of the squatter. The difference

in cost of transit of wheat to the port of ship

ment will b6 sufficient to determine the ques

tion of its profitable occupation for agricultural

purposes. There is a large quantity of first

class land between the line and Moy Hall, the

residence of Mr. W. Robertson, -which might be

famuli to advantage. Mie quantity of wheat

grown year in the immediate neighbourhood

of Narracoorte is considerably less than a few i

years ago, owing "to the working of defective ^

land laws, by which the soil has again found its

way into the hands of the sheepfarmer. Agri- j

cultural' settlement extends to the Moram- ;

bro Creek, a distance of about sixteen

miles to the north, and there are

also farms for about four miles to

the south of Narracoorte. Twenty or thirty

farmers are still left in the area of Binnum and

about T-ftk" Cadnite, but the land to the east

Vmjy mostly fallen into the hands of the squatter*

We believe that there is a considerable quantity

of good land not yet selected lying in a south

eastern direction from the township, and to the

north on the banks of the Morambro Creek and

Lake Cadnite. With the additional conveniences

for traffic afforded by the railway this will be

all farmed, and it is to be hoped that the

increased profit will prevent it from leaving the

hands of the agriculturist. The question of the

probable wool traffic from Victoria has

been practically settled by the partial

experiment already made on the line,

and there is little doubt that in the event of a

branch railway being carried along the border

to the Tatiara country it will drain a large strip

of the Wimmera District, while affording the

settlers of Tatiara a means of communication

between the splendid agricultural land there and

the seaboard. Two lines have been surveyed to

the Tatiara country, one branching out from

the Kingston and Narracoorte Railway at

Baker's Range, and the other proceeding

I northerly nearly parallel with the border, the

latter being the longer, but having the ad

vantage of draining the traffic from the Wim

; mera country, while the former passes almost

entirely through laud which can never be j

I profitably occupied, and will not add to the

I traffic on the railway. The disadvantage of !

the increased length of the line along the

border may be compensated by allowing a

differential rate for produce brought from the

Tatiara country, so -fcnat the Tatiara people

would sustain no practical inconvenience from

the adoption of the longer route, while they

would derive the advantage of a much larger

traffic.

Besides the great increase in the wool traffic

owing to the line being opened, we believe that

since the truck took the place of the coach

between Kingston and Narracoorte the number

of passengers travelling has doubled. Looking

at the whole question, there seems to be a pro

bability of a very fair business for the railway,

i and that the lugubrious prognostications that

the line would never pay for grease for the

wheels is not likely to be realised.

nection with the opening of the railway were

! slightly altered. It was at first intended that two

trains should be dispatched from tins end-one

with the Government party leaving at 9 o'clock,

and another for the general public starting half

an hour later. It was afterwards arranged,

however, that there should be three trains-one

at 7.30 a.m., and one at 9.30 a.m., the Govern

ment carriages following at a later hour j con

sequently the early trains took away a large

number of people from Kingston,and prevented

the display in the way of numbers that would

otherwise have taken place. At the suggestion

of Mrs. E. J. Stuart, a carriage for aboriginals,

of whom there are a considerable number in

the neighbourhood, was attached to one of the

earlier trains.

Mr. Venn read the following address:

"To the Hon. J. Colton, Commissioner of

Public Works, and Members of the Ministry of

South Australia

"We the District Council of Lacepede Bay,

represent!ng the people of our district generally,

give you hearty welcome to Kingston on this

auspicions occasion, and beg to tender our con

gratulations that the Kingston and Narracoorte 1

Railway, so long delayed, is this day ready for

formal opening, and we thank you most cordially

for your presence here for this pxKpose. The

people of this district have every reason to be

grateful to the Parliament that sanctioned this

railway, «""* to the Government for carrying it

out to a successful issue. By a line of 52 miles

in length the worst road in the colony has been

bridged over, and Kingston connected with a

large and important back country. During

the few months that the line has been

open by merely horse-traction, the exports

from Kingston have been trebled, and the im

ports more than quadrupled. It will be inte

resting to you to learn that the up traffic has

increased from 20 tons during the first month

to the pwYimnm of 180 tons per month, the

average being over 80 tons; par month. From

the first opening of the line over 600 tons of

wheat and fiour, previously shut out from the

market on account of the extreme cost of car

riage, have been brought from Narracoorte.

It will gratify you to know that oar exports of

wool have increased from about 4,450 bales last

season to close on 12,500 this season, nearly one

third of which is the produce of Victoria,

turned through this port by the opening of this

line and the facilities given here for direct

shipment to London, by which means the bulk

of the wool has been sent to market this season.

By connecting Border Town by rail a large

area of fine agricultural land in Tatiara will

be profitably utilized, and an immense Vic

torian trade secured to South Australia. If

to this were added the abolition of the Border

duties between Victoria and South Australia,

such a development of trade would ensue

that the events you are now Inaugurating

would become a red-letter day in the history of

the district and of the colony generally. The

loss to South Australian trade will be under

stood when we mention that 150 drays (ap

proximate) which brought Victorian wool to

Narracoorte returned empty in consequence of

the Border restrictions, several woolgrowers

having got supplies from Portland at £7 per ton

carriage. The line will form another link of

communication between Victoria and the

jjaatern colonies by railway, besides aiding in

giving Mount Gaxnbier and the South Australian

southern boundaries daily mail communication

with Adelaide. We believe that the permanent

way of the line reflects the greatest credit on

the Kngineer-in-Chiefs Department, and that

the rolling-stock is all that could be desired.

When are added soife$le ^vgiue-houses, work

eliops, and necessary buildings for passenger

etations/ithen the first-South-Eastern Railway

will be one that South Australia may well be

proud of. We congratulate yon on the steady

progress -of the colony generally, and on

the increasing value of South Australian

securities in the London market, and we

trust that South Australia will soon attain to

that pre-eminence amongst the colonies that

her immense resources entitle her to. We

regret that we have not the pleasure to-day of

expressing our loyalty to the Queen in the

presence of the Governor, hut we can assure you

that we are not behind other parts of the colony

in loyalty to the Queen, in .respect to Her

Majesty's representative. We heartily thank

the Ministry for having brought this railway to

the successful issue to be celebrated to-day, and

for providing a jetty suitable to the- require

ments of the place. We trust the inaugural

proceedings will not be marred by accident, and

wish you a pleasant tour through the district,

and a safe return to Adelaide, feeling sure that

a personal inspection of the district will assist

you greatly in legislating for its present and

future requirements.

man, and the Councillors and Clerk of the

Council.]

The CHIEF SECRETARY, in reply, said:-Mr.

Chairman, Members of the District Council,

and Gentlemen-On behalf of my colleagues and

cipate with regard to this colony will be fully

pected in the future. (Cheers.) One of my

colleagues (Mr. Ward) will accompany me to

morrow and the next day through that portion

being likely to stimulate the trade of

this colony. Mr. Colton and Mr. Carr,

to-day, are going to another district to ascertain

that you have a good opportunity of having

your wants properly represented and fairly ;

looked after when Ministers of the Crown meet

the abolition of the Border duties, I apprehend

it is not meant that we should ask Victoria to

ment should be made between the two Govern

ments whereby certain impediments may be

and Victoria. As you are aware, negotiations

between the two Governments to that end are :

in progress, and Mr. Tyler, a gentleman high in

the Customs Department of Victoria, has met

and approval of the two Governments. So far

we shall have any reason to complain if we are

rupted trade between us. The trade of the line

you conclude your address, I can only say we

are all much obliged to you. (Cheers.)

 jind that Mr. Carr could not refuse the 

 request that had been made for a site of 

 land for ra hospital and for recreation and other 

 purposes/ He trusted that when they lost con

fidence in him they w«uld let him know, so 

 ?hat he oould give place to a worthier represen

tative.

Mr, COITON gave "Prosperity to the Kingston 

 and Narracoorte Railway and the Producing 

 jbiterests of the Colony." In the first place he 

 congratulated them in having a line bridging 

 over such a had part of the country for travel

ling purposes. He believed that there was only ( 

 one opinion as to the construction of the line, 

 and that was that it had been faithfully 

 ?carried out, and would permanently benefit 

 the district. (Cheers.) Since he had 

 jbeen connected with the Public Works 

 ^Department he had gone in for substantial 

 .works, and had been careful to have the per 

 manent ways of the railways carefully made. 

 He had particularly impressed this matter upon 

 .the Engineer-in-Chief; and as required the 

 stations would be improved when the traffic

justified further expenditure. Jetties should

Xlso be made substantially so as to last for many 1 

 years. The money spent in the colony was 

 generally speaking well laid out. As to the 

 -Kingston Jetty, he had formed an opinion that 

 the jetty asked for would only serve the trade 

 ?of that part of the country for a short time. 

 Believing that they should anticipate an 

 increase of business in consequence of 

 ithe construction of public works, he 

 had favoured a good solid structure. (Cheers.) 

 "Without .pledging himself as to the policy of 

 the Government with regard to the extension of 

 the railway line, he would say that it might be 

 necessary some day to go to Border Town. He 

 had seen it stated in the newspapers that the 

 Government were insincere in carrying out the

Bivoli Bay and Mount Gambier Line. That J 

 ?was a .slandering of the Government with- j 

 out cause. He was prepared for slander j 

 from the public Press, but in this par 

 ticular instance there was no ground for it. 

 The members £ot the District of Victoria when 

 Parliament assembled would find that the Go 

 vernment had not been lax. Survey parties had 

 fceen placed on the Bivoli Bay and Mount Gam 

 fcier line, and the Government were endeavour 

 ing to push the work as rapidly as possible. 

 The Drainage "Works were regarded by 

 the Government as exceedingly important. A 

 large quantity of land could be drained 

 with advantage for agricultural purposes. 

 The proper way to represent local matters was 

 by means of deputations. He was quite pre 

 pared to hear of their requirements by deputa 

 tion and through their members, and to grant 

 requests as to public works if they were reason 

 able. (Cheers.) It had been said that a 

 few of the friends of the Government had been 

 invited to that banquet"; but in issuing the 

 invitations he had made no distinction, and had 

 selected representative men as far as possible. 

 He had no favourites in the district; and if any 

 deserving gentleman had been left out in the 

 cold it was an oversight, and he must accept bis 

 apology. (Cheers,)

Mr. H. L. SPRIGG, J.P., in responding, de 

 precated the statement that the railroad 

 was made from a mudhole to a swamp, 

 and maintained that it would prove of great 

 nse in the shipment of produce. It was the 

 commencement of an important network of 

 railways which would make Kingston the great 

 jiort of export for a large part of South Aus

tralia and Victoria.

Mr. JOHN GRICE, J.P., in responding for the 

 commercial interests of the district, said he 

 was indebted to the Government for the accom 

 modation provided by the railway.

Mr. F. Yauq HAS, J.P., responded for the 

 pastoral interest.

Mr. E. J. STTAET, J.P., proposed a The 

 Engineer-in-Chief and Staff/'

Mr. H. C. MAIS, Engineer-in-Chief, responding, 

 apologized for the delay in the travelling that 

 afternoon, it would not occur when the line

got into working order. Great credit was due | 

 jfcQ tb<? officers superintending the construction -

bf the lin£.

After the toast of " The Ladies" and " Til?

Press,'" Mr. Jas. CAEEOL proposed " The Chair- .

man."

The Chaiphan said that any misundersHnd 

 ing in regard to the proceedings was uninten 

 tional, and he was sure from the triumphal and 

 general reception of the Government there was 

 little ill-will to them. He proposed " The Vice 

 chairmen." Mr. H. J. SMITH, S.M., and Mr. 

 THOMAS Hinckley, J.P., responded. The proceed 

 ings then terminated.

THE RETURN TO KINGSTON.

Messrs. Colton, Carr, Wigley, Towusend, 

 Hardy, and Ramsay proceeded to Kingston by 

 special train, and on arrival at once went on 

 "board the Governor Musgrave, which left Lace 

 pede Bay for Robe at daybreak.

Sir Henry Ayers and Mr. "Ward proceeded 

 overland to Melbourne c-n route for Sydney.

[By Electric Telegraph.]

[From our Special Reporter.]

Robe, January 17

The Ministerial party reached Kingston at 

 10.35 last evening, the weather being wet and 

 cold. Messrs. Colton, Carr, Hardy, "Wigley, 

 Townscnd, Ingleby, and Ramsay embarked on 

 Ixwxd the Governor Musgrave, and she left. at 

 4 ^o'clock this morning. The weather was 

 .rough outside, but we made Robe at 8.30 a.m. 

 .this morning. The party did not go ashore till 

 11 o'clock. They were invited to lunch at Mr. J.

Grice's.

The Government flagstaff was gaily decorated 

 .with bunting.

The parly were received by the District 

 Council, who were presented by Mr. A. Hardy, 

 M.P., the member for the district; and the 

 Chairman, Mr. C. Gell, read the following

address:- !

"To the Hon. the Commissioner of Public j

Works and the Members of the Ministry. j 

 " Sir and . Gentlemen - On behalf of the

District Council and the inhabitants of Bobe t 

 we have much pleasure in bidding you welcome ; 

 to Robe. As a part of the South-Eastern | 

 District we join in congratulating you and the 

 country on the opening of the Kingston and 

 Narracoorte Railway, hoping that the first 

 .-railway ill the district may prove successful and 

 fulfil tlie best hopes of its friends. "We look 

 upon the South-East as an importaut part of 

 iSouth Australia, and look forward ,to the time 

 when additional means of communication may 

 he provided for developing its resources.

" Hoping that at some future time we may 

 ?have the pleasure of another and longer visit

from you,

"We remain, Sir, your obedient servants,

" Chas. GELL, Chairman of the District

Council of Kobe."

(Signed also by the members and Clerk of the

Council.)

The COMMISSIONER of PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. 

 J. Colton) in reply tendered thanks on behalf of 

 liimself and his colleagues for the honour done 

 .?them on the present occasion in the address 

 welcoming them to the district. It was pleasing 

 -to meet gentlemen of various districts, and the 

 visit was a very agreeable one. It was thought, 

 .in conversation with the members for the dis 

 jfcrict, that the visit would be agreeable, and 

 hence it was determined upon. He hoped the 

 anticipations in connection with the railway 

 now opened would be realized, and that it would 

 ?develop largely the fine land they had in the 

 South-East. He had for years considered it one 

 of the finest parts of the colony. The Ministry 

 had begun the railway policy, and he was sure 

 the people would endorse its prosecution. He was 

 .glad that he had had an opportunity of meeting 

 ihem, and on his next visit he hoped be should

lave more time at his command.

The oompany then sat down to luncheon, the 

 ^Chairman of the District Council (Mr. Gell) 

 presiding, having the Hon. J. Colton on his 

 light, and the Hon. J. Carr on his left.

After the usual loyal toasts bad been dis

jposedof,

The Chairman proposed "The Ministry."

JTe did not think the Kingston and Narracoorfce 

 Railway would do Robe good, still it would dp 

 no harm, and he wasglad to see the trade coming 

 that way, and he hoped some day that Sobe 

 might apply for a railway, and by that means 

 show her prosperity. He hoped the Ministry 

 would continue to hold office, so as to push for 

 ward the policy of development and immigra

tion.

Mr. Corms replied. He said he believed it 

 was without exception the desire of the Ministry 

 to do the best they could for the development 

 of the country. He had never met a number of 

 men who had worked better together than the 

 Ministry, and their schemes were thus more

likely to succeed. Of Sir Henry Ayers it had . 

 been said that he was not progressive, but he 

 had found him as much so as pru 

 dence permitted. - He had much to thank 

 that gentleman for in departmental and 

 general matters connected with the Govern 

 ment of the country. The railways already 

 authorized were important, but they were only 

 initiative. In order to be a great nation it was 

 necessary that the public men should have broad 

 and large views. The public men of the present 

 time he had found to be possessed of such views, 

 and he was sure they would assist in maturing 

 useful measures. He had never felt stronger 

 mentally, and perhaps physically, than at 

 present; but the duties of his office were very 

 onerous at present because he was desirous of 

 bringing the work passed to a successful issue 

 without waste of money, but yet substantially. 

 He was glad he had introduced two or three 

 men whose services would be of importance to 

 the country, and with the Engineer-in-Chief he 

 knew he had men who would carry out the 

 views of the Government. "When engineering 

 difficulties existed he was always willing to 

 give way, but where a work was absolutely 

 necessary he put everything else on one 

 side, and said it must be carried out, and 

 this -fras done as far as it was possible. He 

 and his colleague were much pleased with their 

 reception, and hoped to see Robe connected 

 with other parts of the colony in the network 

 of railways. He returned thanks for the toast.

The CHAIRMAN proposed " The Parliament," 

 naming the members for the district and ex 

 pressing the satisfaction of the constituency

with them.

Mr. W. TOWNSEND, M.P., replied, saying that 

 he hoped Sobe had reached its worst and would

soon see better times.

Mr. A. HABDT, M.P., said he was glad to hear 

 that Robe had no burning wants which would 

 make the people very energetic in seeking to 

 have them dealt with. The place wanted an 

 increase of business, but it would attain this by 

 means of the settlement of land in the neigh 

 bourhood, and especcially through the Drainage 

 Works. The jetty had been handed to the 

 Council by the Government; but although it 

 yielded a good revenue there was also much 

 expenditure necessary in connection with it, 

 and he thought it would be better that the 

 Government should resume possession. If a 

 request to this effect were forwarded to Mr. 

 "Wigley and himself it would be laid before the

authorities.

Sir. W. R. "WIGLEY, M.P., said it was very 

 pleasing to hear from the people of Robe that 

 they were satisfied with him, as they had asked 

 him to enter Parliament as their representative. 

 He could not say that the place had progressed, 

 ! but he hoped that the silver lining to the cloud

j would soon appear. He and his colleague would

use all their endeavours to further the interests

of the district. The fares by the Melbourne 

 steamers might be advantageously lessened, and 

 then salubrious Robe would be adopted as the 

 chief South Australian watering place. If he 

 had satisfied the district he should return to it

for re-election.

Mr. COLTON proposed "The Health of the 

 Chairman" in complimentary terms.

The Chairmas returned thanks, hoping that 

 the good days for Robe would come again, and 

 advised the gentlemen of Adelaide to build sea 

 residences there, and he hoped Mr. "Wigley

would be the first to do so.

Mr. TOVTXSEXD proposed "The Host and

Hostess."

Tli^^entlemeh representing Robe present at the

luncheon were Messrs. W. Warren, D. Grosse,

J. "Watson, "W. Savage, A. Tolmer, R, Westiatid, 

 and H. AVylie.

A visit was afterwards paid to the Gaol, and 

 after inspecting the arrangements the party 

 proceeded to tbe beach, and Mr. Colton fired a 

 life-saving rocket over the lifeboat shed, a 

 distance of 200 yards.

The visitors were then entertained at luncheon 

 by Mr. J. Grice, J.P.

The Musgrave left Guichen Bay at about 3 

 o'clock p.m., and expected to be at Eivoli Bay 

 in the. evening.

MBTA and Keolis Announce Commuter Rail Schedule Adjustments
===========================================================

Posted on July 9, 2025
----------------------

**Changes on the Fall River/New Bedford, Greenbush, Kingston, and Providence/Stoughton Lines to take effect on July 21**

* * *

The MBTA and Keolis Commuter Services (Keolis), the operations and maintenance partner for the Commuter Rail, will implement minor schedule adjustments for four Commuter Rail lines to improve reliability for passengers, particularly on the new Fall River/New Bedford Line. The updated schedules will take effect on July 21 for the Fall River/New Bedford, Greenbush, Kingston, and Providence/Stoughton Lines.

Rail Service Over the Years
===========================

By: Latonya Linton, August 30, 2022

Listen

[Transport](https://jis.gov.jm/news?category=transport)

![Image 5: Rail Service Over the Years](https://jis.gov.jm/media/2022/08/Photo-7.jpg?v=1661904065)

###### Photo: Dave Reid

 Students participate in the rollout of the School Train Service, at the Spanish Town Train Station in St. Catherine, on January 10. 

The Full Story
--------------

Jamaica’s railway system is one of the oldest in the world, with the first tracks laid in 1845, connecting Kingston to Angels in St. Catherine.

The proposal to construct the first railway line was made to the House of Assembly in Jamaica in 1843 by William Smith and his brother David Smith. Construction commenced in 1844 under the name, Railway Company, which was a private entity.

Over the years, the railway service played a vital role in providing passenger and freight services to the agricultural and mining sectors.

Some of the routes opened included Spanish Town to Old Harbour (1869), Old Harbour to Porus and Angels to Ewarton (1855), and Porus to Montego Bay (1894).

Other routes included Bog Walk to Port Antonio (1896), May Pen to Chapelton (1913), Linstead to New Works (1921), Chapelton to Frankfield (1925) and Logan’s Junction to Vernamfield in Clarendon (1941).

Ownership of the railway changed hands among private owners several times over the decades, until in 1960, just two years before the country achieved Independence on August 6, 1962, when the Government turned over the management of the railway to the newly established Jamaica Railway Corporation (JRC).

![Image 6: A yellow train at a train station with people walking around](https://jis.gov.jm/media/2022/08/IMG-20210526-WA0047-500x243.jpg)

A passenger train prepares to leave the Spanish Town Railway Station in St. Catherine.

The JRC was established under the Jamaica Railway Corporation Act.

“The Government saw it necessary to establish a Railway Act, which gives the power to do whatever is necessary to operate a rail service, because the existing legislation at the time did not allow us to do that. Other than establish the Railway Act, it allows the Jamaica Railway Corporation to be a little more flexible in its operation,” Consultant Engineer at the JRC, Anthony Allen, tells JIS News.

When the JRC took control of the country’s rail network, the primary cargo of the trains was agricultural produce, before eventually transitioning to primarily transporting bauxite for local companies along various routes.

“With the advent of the bauxite companies, a much more lucrative revenue earner, the emphasis was really to move cargo for the bauxite company between Port Esquivel, May Pen to Williamsfield, Bodles through to Spanish town and up to Ewarton,” Mr. Allen informs.

In 1969, passenger traffic using trains along the now long and numerous routes across the country was more than one million per year. However, by 1973 an issue that has plagued the railway system since its origin re-emerged, that of operating capital.

According to ‘The History of Railroads/ways in Jamaica’, written by the National Library of Jamaica, by 1975 the financial crisis led to an inability to keep up with maintenance of trains and lines, and in 1974 the May Pen to Frankfield line closed, followed by the Bog Walk to Port Antonio line in 1975.

Public passenger service ceased operating in Jamaica in October 1992.

“It was basically an economic decision because passengers really cannot pay for the wear and tear of the railway and the maintenance of both the locomotives and the tracks and the infrastructure in general. So, passenger trains really have to be subsidised and over the years the issue became more and more… as the equipment aged, as the track aged, and, therefore, it proved to be very uneconomical to continue to move passengers,” Mr. Allen explains.

By April 2011, the service was restarted along the May Pen to Linstead route but was stopped again.

In 2022, trains made another comeback with the introduction of a pilot Student Passenger Rail Service to provide safe and cost-effective transportation to students from Old Harbour and Linstead to Spanish Town.

Six schools participated in the programme, where the trains carried more than 66 per cent of their capacity, transporting a combined total of 16,683 students on two round trips per day during the pilot.

For his part, Minister of Transport and Mining, Hon. Audley Shaw, says the Government is committed to getting the trains rolling again and is prepared to forge the necessary partnerships in the undertaking.

Speaking recently during a tour of the JRC terminus in West Kingston, Mr. Shaw noted that revival of islandwide rail service will take “several hundred millions of US dollars” and will include “putting in a new bridge to go to Spanish Town, and that alone is going to cost about US$8 million”.

Long-delayed £1bn train fleet to launch
=======================================

28 November 2024

ShareSave

Paul CliftonBBC South transport correspondent

ShareSave

![Image 1](https://static.files.bbci.co.uk/bbcdotcom/web/20251210-151139-37baf2dfdd-web-2.36.1-1/grey-placeholder.png)![Image 2: South Western Railway Exterior shot of an Arterio train with South Western Railway branding](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/7568/live/33ce6a50-acd2-11ef-bdf5-b7cb2fa86e10.png.webp)South Western Railway

The new Arterio train fleet had been due to start running in 2019

An event to mark the rollout of long-delayed new trains for South Western Railway will be held later.

The Derby-built Class 701 Arterio trains are five years behind schedule.

Ninety trains, costing £1bn, were ordered in 2017 and were due in service from November 2019.

The trains were held up by extensive faults, mostly to do with software. Many have spent years stored in sidings.

The RMT union held 78 days of strikes about the role of guards on these trains before reaching an agreement with the train operator.

The first Arterio train carried passengers between London Waterloo and Windsor in January 2024.

The "development" service was mostly restricted to one return trip a day outside peak hours. Since then, only a few trains have appeared in regular service.

South Western Railway (SWR) said more trains would start work on other routes in the coming weeks.

It is training 750 drivers to operate them.

![Image 3](https://static.files.bbci.co.uk/bbcdotcom/web/20251210-151139-37baf2dfdd-web-2.36.1-1/grey-placeholder.png)![Image 4: Interior view of an Arterio train, showing no doors between carriages](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/afcb/live/298b59d0-acd3-11ef-a4fe-a3e9a6c5d640.jpg.webp)

The trains are designed to hold more passengers

Earlier this year, the BBC used the Freedom of Information Act to try to uncover the total public cost of the delay, including the additional cost of keeping older trains running.

But the Department for Transport responded that, although it did hold the information, it would not reveal the cost.

It said the number would "prejudice the commercial interests of South Western Railway and the department".
